The summary of costs and benefits of the proposed standard considered only quantifiable expenditures and savings relating to the standard. Although Ford is correct that there may be some additional costs of the improved fuel economy in terms of reduced utility, these nonquantifiable costs were not contained in the summary of costs and benefits. Since the final rule, like the proposed rule, is based upon the manufacturers' product plans for model year 1979, these performance costs are not expected to be great.
Ford contended that meeting the average fuel economy standards would result in an average retail price equivalent increase of at least $100.00 per vehicle, if the proposed standard of 18.7 mpg were not reduced for emissions and testing penalties. Since the final standard reflects a substantial reduction from the proposed standard of 8 percent, due to the change in the fuel economy testing procedures, the agency assumes that the estimated price increase of $100.00 is no longer applicable. Although some price increase may be likely to meet the final standard, there is nothing in the Ford comment to indicate that the NHTSA estimate of $24.00 per vehicle retail price increase ($12 cost to the manufacturer, with a markup of 100 percent) is an incorrect estimate of that increase.
